taxes.base: Employment, self-employment, pension, savings, dividend and property income of individuals, after the personal allowance.
taxes.payer: Individuals; employers deduct it from pay (PAYE).

rate.headline: 20% / 40% / 45% (Scotland: 19%–48%)
details: England, Wales and Northern Ireland, 2026-27: 0% up to the £12,570 Personal Allowance, 20% to £50,270, 40% to £125,140, 45% above. The allowance is withdrawn at £1 for every £2 of income over £100,000.
Scotland sets its own rates and bands for non-savings, non-dividend income (six bands from 19% to 48%); Wales has a Welsh rate that is currently the same as England’s.
Savings and dividend income have their own rates and allowances.

instruments.explanation: The largest source of revenue. PAYE deducted from pay is about 85% of the total. Figures here include Scottish and Welsh income tax, which HMRC collects.
exceptions: Pensions and ISAs are tax-advantaged within limits.

taxes.base: Employees’ earnings (employee contributions), employers’ payroll (employer contributions) and the profits of the self-employed.

rate.headline: Employees 8% / 2%; employers 15%
details: Class 1, 2026-27: employees pay 8% on earnings between £12,570 and £50,270 and 2% above; employers pay 15% on earnings above £5,000 a year (raised from 13.8% and a £9,100 threshold in April 2025).
Self-employed pay Class 4 on profits and, voluntarily, Class 2.

instruments.explanation: A payroll-based charge that funds the contributory state pension and the NHS. Revenue rose sharply in 2025-26 because of the higher employer rate and lower threshold.
exceptions: Employment allowance for small employers; no contributions on earnings under the lower limits.

taxes.base: Most supplies of goods and services by registered businesses and imports.
taxes.payer: Consumers; businesses charge it and deduct input tax.

rate.headline: 20% standard; 5% reduced; 0% zero-rated
details: Zero rate on most food, books, children’s clothes and public transport; 5% on domestic fuel; private school fees became standard-rated from January 2025.

instruments.explanation: The second-largest tax. Revenue is shown net of refunds.
exceptions: Exempt: financial services, health, education and rent. Registration threshold of £90,000 turnover.

taxes.base: Profits of companies and other bodies, including capital gains of companies.

rate.headline: 25%; 19% for small profits
details: 25% on profits above £250,000; 19% on profits up to £50,000; marginal relief in between.
Full expensing of qualifying plant and machinery.

instruments.explanation: The main rate has been 25% since April 2023 (it was 19% before); revenue has risen with profits and the higher rate.

taxes.base: Gains on the disposal of assets such as shares and second homes, above an annual exempt amount.

details: 18% for gains within the basic rate band and 24% above it (from 30 October 2024); the annual exempt amount is £3,000.

instruments.explanation: Revenue nearly doubled in 2025-26 after rates were raised and the exempt amount cut.

taxes.base: Petrol, diesel and other road fuels, by the litre.
taxes.payer: Fuel suppliers; passed on at the pump.

rate.headline: 52.95p per litre of petrol and diesel (2025-26)
details: The rate has been frozen for years, with a temporary 5p cut; the Treasury has scheduled it to be restored gradually.

instruments.explanation: A per-litre duty that has not risen with inflation since 2011.
exceptions: Reduced rates for gas oil used off-road (red diesel), with exceptions.

names.official: Stamp taxes (stamp duty land tax, stamp duty reserve tax, stamp duty, ATED)

taxes.base: Purchases of land and buildings in England and Northern Ireland (SDLT), transfers of shares (stamp duty and SDRT) and high-value dwellings held by companies (ATED).

rate.headline: SDLT 0%–12%; shares 0.5%
details: SDLT from April 2025: nil to £125,000, 2% to £250,000, 5% to £925,000, 10% to £1.5 million, 12% above; first-time buyers pay nothing to £300,000. A 5% surcharge applies to additional dwellings.
Shares: 0.5% stamp duty or SDRT.

instruments.explanation: Stamp duty land tax is £14.8 billion of the total. Scotland and Wales run their own taxes on property transactions.

taxes.base: Beer, wine, cider and spirits by volume of alcohol.
taxes.payer: Producers and importers; passed on in the price.

rate.headline: Per litre of pure alcohol, by strength
details: Since August 2023 a single duty rate per litre of alcohol applies to all drinks, with lower rates for draught products and small producers; rates rise with RPI each February.

instruments.explanation: A unified duty on all alcoholic drinks by strength.

taxes.base: Premiums on most general insurance (motor, home, travel, pet).

rate.headline: 12% standard; 20% higher rate
details: 12% on most insurance; 20% on travel insurance and insurance sold with some goods.

instruments.explanation: A tax on premiums that stands in for VAT on insurance, which is exempt.
exceptions: Life, health and long-term care insurance are exempt.

taxes.base: The estate of a person who dies and some lifetime gifts, above the nil-rate bands.
taxes.payer: The estate; some trusts and gifts pay on their own account.

rate.headline: 40% above the nil-rate band
details: 40% on the value above £325,000, plus a £175,000 residence nil-rate band; transfers to a spouse are exempt. The thresholds are frozen until 2030 and pensions are due to come within the tax from April 2027.

instruments.explanation: A small tax in revenue terms but large in political attention: only a small share of estates (around 4–5%) pay it.
exceptions: Business and agricultural property relief is being restricted from April 2026.

taxes.base: Cigarettes, hand-rolling tobacco and other tobacco products.
taxes.payer: Producers and importers; passed on in the price.

rate.headline: Per 1,000 cigarettes plus a share of the price
details: Duty rises each year by RPI plus 2%; hand-rolling tobacco rises faster.

instruments.explanation: Revenue is falling as smoking declines.

taxes.base: Imported goods, by tariff heading and origin.

rate.headline: UK Global Tariff
details: Rates are set in the UK Global Tariff; many goods are free under trade agreements.

instruments.explanation: Since 2021 the UK has its own tariff.

taxes.base: Passengers departing from UK airports, by distance band and class of travel.

rate.headline: Per passenger by distance band and class
details: Rates rise each April; higher for premium cabins and private jets.

instruments.explanation: A per-passenger tax on flights.
exceptions: Children under 16 in economy are exempt.

taxes.base: Employers’ annual pay bill above £3 million.

rate.headline: 0.5% of the pay bill above £3 million
details: A £15,000 annual allowance is set against the levy.

instruments.explanation: A payroll levy that funds apprenticeship training.

taxes.base: Gross profits of betting and gaming operators and the stakes of some bets.

rate.headline: By type of gambling
details: General betting duty, remote gaming duty, pool betting duty, gaming duty and bingo duty each have their own rate; the Budget raised some of them.

instruments.explanation: Duties on the profits of the gambling industry.

names.official: Sector and environmental levies (energy profits levy, climate change levy, bank levy and surcharge, digital services tax and others)

taxes.base: Oil and gas profits, energy use, bank balance sheets and profits, digital platform revenues, landfill, aggregates, soft drinks, plastic packaging and developers’ profits.

rate.headline: A different rate for each levy
details: Energy profits levy £2.6 billion, climate change levy £1.8 billion, bank levy £1.7 billion, bank surcharge £1.2 billion, digital services tax £1.1 billion, diverted profits tax £0.6 billion, landfill tax £0.5 billion, aggregates levy £0.4 billion, soft drinks industry levy £0.4 billion, plastic packaging tax £0.3 billion and smaller ones.

instruments.explanation: A group of targeted taxes on particular industries and activities.

taxes.base: Ownership of a vehicle on the road, by CO₂ emissions (first year) and a flat rate afterwards.

rate.headline: First-year rate by CO₂; then a standard rate
details: Electric cars have paid VED since 1 April 2025; an expensive-car supplement applies to cars over £40,000 in the first five years after the first year.

instruments.explanation: The annual road tax, collected by the DVLA.

names.official: Scottish Income Tax (Scottish rates of income tax)

taxes.base: Non-savings, non-dividend income of Scottish taxpayers.

rate.headline: Six bands from 19% to 48%
details: The Scottish Parliament sets the rates and bands; the UK government sets the personal allowance. Scottish taxpayers with higher incomes pay more than elsewhere in the UK.

instruments.explanation: Included in the UK income tax figure above: HMRC collects it and passes it to the Scottish Government, adjusted by a reconciliation after the outturn is known.

taxes.base: Purchases of land and buildings in Scotland.

rate.headline: Bands set by the Scottish Parliament
details: Residential and non-residential rates and bands differ from stamp duty land tax; an Additional Dwelling Supplement applies.

instruments.explanation: Scotland’s own replacement for stamp duty land tax, collected by Revenue Scotland.

taxes.base: Purchases of land and buildings in Wales.

rate.headline: Bands set by the Senedd
details: Residential, higher-rate (additional dwellings) and non-residential rates are set in Wales.

instruments.explanation: Wales’s own replacement for stamp duty land tax, collected by the Welsh Revenue Authority.

names.official: Council Tax (and domestic rates in Northern Ireland)

taxes.base: Domestic dwellings, by valuation band (values of 1991 in England and Scotland, 2003 in Wales).
taxes.payer: The resident or owner of the dwelling; discounts for single occupants.

rate.headline: Set by each council by band
details: Councils set an annual charge for each valuation band (A to H, A to I in Wales); in England increases above a limit (just under 5% for most councils in 2025-26) need a local referendum.

instruments.explanation: The main local tax, billed by around 300 English billing authorities and the Scottish and Welsh councils. It funds about half of English councils’ spending.
exceptions: Students and people on low incomes get discounts or support.

taxes.base: The rateable value of non-domestic property (shops, offices, factories).

rate.headline: Rateable value × a national multiplier
details: The Government sets the multiplier each year; a 2026 revaluation updated rateable values in April 2026, and lower multipliers apply to retail, hospitality and leisure.
Councils keep 62% of the income locally and 38% goes to the Treasury.

instruments.explanation: A national tax that councils collect: set by Parliament, collected locally and partly redistributed.
exceptions: Reliefs of £7.7 billion in 2025-26 (small business, retail, hospitality and leisure).
